title: Looped Propeller Design Aims to Reduce Noise Near Whales
summary:
A Detroit-based company called Sharrow Marine is partnering with marine conservation organization Ocean Alliance to test quieter boat propellers on research expeditions near whales. The work is still at an early stage, but it could help explore a way to reduce underwater noise from boats.

Noise pollution is not limited to crowded streets. Large shipping boats, deep-sea mining equipment and offshore oil rigs have changed the ocean's sound environment. Whales rely on calls to coordinate with one another, find food and locate mates. When the water is quiet, they can hear calls from hundreds of miles away. However, commercial shipping produces noise that overlaps with the low-frequency sounds whales use to communicate.

Michelle Fournet, an acoustic ecologist and ocean noise pollution expert at the University of New Hampshire, described this interference to Popular Science. She compared persistent ocean noise to someone repeatedly using a jackhammer outside a window. Research described in the source also linked louder noise around orcas with a lower chance of catching fish they chased.

Much of the disruptive noise from boat propellers comes from cavitation. When a screw-shaped propeller spins quickly, tiny bubbles form behind it. As these bubbles pop, they release energy and create hissing or crackling sounds. A single propeller can produce and pop millions of bubbles per second.

Sharrow's design replaces blades with free-standing tips with looped blades that twist like a ribbon. The company says the design produces fewer tip vortices, or swirling flows at the blade tips, reducing cavitation. It claims independent testing showed underwater noise reductions of up to seven decibels in the frequency range whales use to communicate. Decibels measure sound levels. These are company-reported findings; the source does not provide the full testing methods or results.

Greg Sharrow, the company's founder and CEO, says the amount of noise reduction varies with frequency, application and operating conditions. Measurements above water also cannot establish how much quieter a boat sounds to whales underwater. That distinction matters when assessing possible benefits for marine animals.

The idea originally grew from Sharrow's work recording orchestras. He wanted to film a violinist using a camera drone inside an orchestra, but its buzzing interfered with the music. Thinking about a propeller without separate blade tips led him to consider boats too. Early prototypes were tested in a fish tank. He says he made more than 640 prototypes before partnering with the University of Michigan, which led to testing on a small boat.

Ocean Alliance CEO Iain Kerr supports approaches that benefit the environment, animals and boat users. Greg Sharrow believes quieter vessel noise could help marine animals hear one another with less interference. The research partnership is exploring the design near whales; benefits for their communication have not yet been established in the supplied report.
why_it_matters: The design offers a possible way to reduce boat noise that overlaps with whale calls. Underwater testing matters because quieter sound above water alone cannot establish benefits for whales.
